description: Hey there, I am from the Technology Innovation Management Master's program at Carleton University, working on building a solution for healthcare software for astronauts.
summary:
We created Oxygen Assessment, a NASA Space Apps prototype that helps users explore oxygen saturation, heart rate, and respiratory rate through an interactive web application. It demonstrates how understandable health information could support astronauts working with limited immediate ground support.

The app replays real HAPP research observations, allowing users to select participants, move through recorded measurements, inspect trends, and view forecasts. It includes explanations of model contributions, forecast history, contextual notes, review prompts, five educational guidance cards, and an embedded tutorial. Recorded measurements and predictions are distinguished, and future observations remain hidden during replay.

Behind the interface, we built a reproducible Python pipeline for checking data quality, preparing forecasting examples, and evaluating models with separate training, validation, and test participants. The selected Ridge regression model uses the preceding 60 seconds of measurements to predict average oxygen saturation over the next 30 seconds. Across four test participants, its average absolute error was approximately 0.48 percentage points, compared with 0.57 for the persistence baseline.

It remains a research demonstration using terrestrial chamber data; clinical effectiveness and performance with astronauts have not been established through validation.
details:
Our project, Oxygen Assessment, is a web-based research prototype designed to help astronauts understand changes in oxygen saturation and related physiological measurements when immediate medical consultation may be limited. It brings oxygen saturation, heart rate, respiratory rate, short-term forecasts, and educational guidance into one accessible interface.

Users can explore historical recordings, review recent changes, and see a prediction of average oxygen saturation over the next 30 seconds using the preceding 60 seconds of measurements. They can also explore what influenced the estimate and enter symptoms, activity, or measurement concerns for the selected snapshot. These notes remain separate from the recorded measurements and model predictions.

We developed the forecasting pipeline in Python, using NumPy, pandas, and scikit-learn. We compared Ridge regression with a simple baseline that assumes oxygen saturation stays at its current value. Across four held-out test participants, Ridge achieved an average absolute error of approximately 0.48 oxygen-saturation percentage points, compared with 0.57 for the baseline. Our data came from the HAPP terrestrial chamber study involving 20 participants; it is not astronaut telemetry.

The interface uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, and Recharts, with hosting on Netlify. We used pytest, Vitest, Playwright, and axe for automated verification. The prototype runs in a browser without an account, installation, or additional hardware, and uses precomputed forecasts without requiring a live AI service.

The creative aspect is how the project connects forecasting with understandable explanations and context. Users can distinguish recorded measurements, calculated changes, model estimates, personal notes, and sourced guidance. This helps them understand where information comes from and what it can tell them.

Our intended impact is to support more informed, independent review of physiological changes and provide a foundation for future astronaut health tools. During development, we considered accessibility, privacy, communication constraints, data quality, and the risk of misleading users. We separated participants across training, validation, and testing, prevented future observations from entering prediction inputs, and kept demonstration notes in temporary session memory. The current project is a proof of concept; clinical and astronaut validation would be necessary before operational use.
